mappings.note: Asks the student to contrast a guess with a reasoned expectation and say what reasoning would improve it - that is LO-7 (prediction plus the reasoning behind it), not LO-6 (framing a testable question). LO-10 is added because the examples offered (cricket result, weather) are exactly the complex systems whose predictions stay uncertain.
The judgement asked for is when an approximate value suffices versus when precision is required - the reasonableness half of LO-9. Not LO-7: nothing is being predicted, a quantity is being sized.

Requires naming a real object or problem that needs at least two branches - the literal demand of LO-3. Not LO-4, which is about science meeting non-science domains; here every branch named is inside science.

Careful observation and noticing patterns is the magnifying-glass half of the chapter's framing symbol. No learning outcome in this curriculum names observation, so the mapping sits at the inquiry competency, which covers using instruments and drawing inferences from data. Flagged as a weak fit.

The compass stands for two named things - asking the right questions (LO-6) and choosing appropriate models while knowing their limits (LO-7). Its sibling question on the magnifying glass gets neither, because observation is not what the compass symbolises.
Straight definition of a model as a deliberate simplification - LO-7. Not LO-8: the question never varies the question being asked, it asks what a model is for.

Why the detailed object is replaced by a geometric one - the 'states which details it ignores and why' clause of LO-7. LO-8 would apply if the item turned on a change of question; here the purpose is fixed and only the representation changes.
Asks what the simplified representation of a car actually is (a point). That is the representation itself, LO-7, rather than the relevance judgement of LO-8.

Four models are judged valid or not by whether the variables kept match the phenomenon being studied - the question decides which details are relevant, which is LO-8 exactly. LO-7 alone cannot decide the item, because every model listed is simplified; only relevance separates them.
Names the detail a standard model drops (air resistance) and why - LO-7. No competing question is offered, so LO-8 does not apply.

The stem fixes a question ('does it cross the boundary') and asks which detail is therefore essential - LO-8, relevance set by the question. Its twin item on what can be dropped is mapped to LO-7 instead.

Mirror of the previous item but asked from the ignoring side - what the model leaves out and why it is safe to. That is LO-7's 'states which details it ignores'; LO-8 is reserved here for the include-side item.
Saha's star as hot gas is the model itself - a deliberately simplified representation, LO-7. Not C5.2-LO-5: the item credits one named individual, so it is not about collective effort.
Asks specifically what Saha left out, the 'which details it ignores and why' clause of LO-7. Kept distinct from the companion item by the ignoring focus rather than the representation focus.

Statements 1-2 are about terms carrying unambiguous meaning (LO-6); statement 3, the one that makes the key, is about quantities having defined standard units (C5.2-LO-6). Both are needed to settle the item.
Why an international standard for the kilogram exists - the 'arose from international agreement' half of LO-6. Not C7.1-LO-6, which concerns words rather than units.
The role of mathematics as compact statements of how quantities relate is LO-7 verbatim. Not C5.2-LO-6: no symbol or unit convention is at issue, only what an equation does.
Scored by pairing quantity, symbol and SI unit correctly - the 'uses SI units correctly' clause of LO-6. Not LO-7: no relationship between quantities is expressed.
The aircraft case is the consequence of not using agreed units - LO-6. The item asks only what the error was, so no estimation outcome (LO-9) is engaged even though a calculation went wrong.

Fairness in trade is the stem's own emphasis, so alongside LO-6 this earns C5.2-LO-4 - scientific convention operating outside science. Its sibling items on units stay on LO-6 alone because they stay inside the laboratory.

The reason clause is purely historical etymology for a symbol, which is the 'arose from history' half of LO-6. Nothing here concerns everyday-versus-scientific word meaning, so C7.1-LO-6 does not apply.

The key is that science converts the claim into questions about measurable physical or chemical change - LO-6, framing a testable question and rejecting one that cannot be settled by evidence. The later item on why the claim actually fails is mapped to C5.2-LO-4 instead.
The exact defined value of c is a fact of international agreement about units, LO-6. It is not LO-7: no relationship between quantities is being expressed.

Asks what a law does as distinct from a theory or a principle - the discrimination LO-4 names. The distractors are precisely theory and model, confirming that the discrimination, not the content, is tested.

Same discrimination as the previous item but applied to examples: the student must reject atomic theory (a theory), energy conservation (a principle) and Saha's model to pick Newton's laws. That is LO-4 at the example level.
